6 The Bayesian Statistics Paradigm

6.1 Introduction to Bayesian statistics

  • •

    In general, the goal of statistics is to make an inference (i.e. to answer questions about real world quantities of interest, test hypotheses, etc.) using observed data, x.

  • •

    To do this, the data is assumed to have originated from a probability model f⁢(x|θ), and our inference is (usually) expressed in terms of an unobservable parameter θ of the distribution f.

  • •

    Thus, under this general framework we can construct and appraise arguments that reason from data to scientific conclusions about the problem or system which generated that data. These conclusions are typically statements in terms of statistical models we have constructed, the parameters introduced in those models (and their values), or the distributions underlying them.

Aside: Probability, logic, and subjectivism

As mathematicians, perhaps we should consider that formal logic should be the most appropriate route to such problems of inference. However, formal logic offers no way to reason about uncertain statements because it can only assign two ‘truth values’ to simple propositions or statements: either a statement is true or it is false, corresponding to certainty one way or the other. What we need is a more general and more flexible form of ‘logic’ that assigns ‘degrees of plausibility’ to uncertain statements, including certainty one way or the other as two extreme cases.

A theorem by Cox22 2 See  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cox’s_theorem  says that (if we make three not-too-crazy assumptions) the only way to construct such a general form of logic is to use probability as this quantification of the ‘degree of plausibility’ of an uncertain statement, and to use the rules of probability theory to manipulate those probabilities and evaluate the strength of the arguments. While it is reassuring that such a result reinforces basing all of our methods in terms of probability, it does raise the question of where these probabilities come from, and what they mean? Depending on how you answer this question leads to two different approaches to statistics.

A natural approach33 3 Other approaches are available. to address the question of where probabilities come from and what they mean is to adopt a subjective view of probability. Without wanting to stray too far into the philosophical foundations of probability, one of the forefathers of Bayesian statistics, Bruno De Finetti, wrote in his classic book, The Theory of Probability, that “Probability does not exist.” Probability has no objective existence or definition, and it is neither a feature of the world around us, nor some fundamental physical property (like mass or energy) that can be measured. If probability does not objectively exist, then it can only be something that we have subjectively constructed to reason about uncertainty. Therefore, under a subjective viewpoint probability can only be a personal quantification of degree of belief of an event occurring. It is subjective, since your belief, my belief, and anyone else’s belief could all be different. However, while the probability values may differ, the usual laws of probability do not change and provide us with the means to manipulate and reason with those probabilities in a coherent, rational, and consistent manner.

  • •

    How we view the data and the parameters is fundamental to how the machinery of statistics operates.

  • •

    Thus far, we have seen the standard approach to statistics, where our methods are based exclusively on arguments of likelihood. To highlight and review the key features of this approach to statistical problems, we will use the following illustrative example.

Example: Drug Trial

In a drug trial, the effects of the drug amiloride on patients with cystic fibrosis were investigated. 16 patients were enrolled in a trial and randomly allocated to the drug and placebo (alternately, so each patient experiences both). Of the 16 patients, 11 showed an improvement in lung function on the drug rather than the placebo. What inference can we make about the effectiveness of the drug?

The Frequentist approach to statistics

  • •

    The Frequentist (also likelihood or classical or standard) approach to statistics adopts the view that only the data, x, is random (before being observed, of course).

Example: Drug Trial

We have a simple binomial scenario, so we can assume X∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(16,p), where X is the total number of patients who improved during the trial and θ=p is the success probability parameter. Before we see the data X=x, the variable X is unknown, and we can write the probability mass function of obtaining this value of the data as

f⁢(x|p)=(16x)⁢px⁢(1−p)16−x,

which is a function of the future unseen data, x, and p is treated as a fixed but unknown value.

  • •

    Note that we can only express a probability statement about an unknown variable. In the likelihood approach to statistics, only the data X are random, and parameters θ are viewed as unknown but constant. Consequently, probability distributions can only be placed on the data, not the parameters.

  • •

    Given this setup, we then observe the data X=x and return to the probability f⁢(x|θ) above, where we fix x to be the value observed and treat the probability44 4 Note, however, that as a probability statement this is no longer valid as X is no longer a random variable once it has been observed, and θ was constant to begin with. as a function of θ. This is now the likelihood function, ℓ⁢(θ)=f⁢(x|θ), and we maximise ℓ⁢(θ) to get the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE).

Example: Drug Trial

We have that:

p^MLE=p^=x/n=11/16=0.69.

p^MLE is the value of p that makes the data most likely to occur under this binomial model.

  • •

    Thus by following this process we have asked and answered the question:

What value of θ makes the data most likely to occur under the assumed data-generating model?

  • •

    However, here we encounter the first issue in the frequentist approach to statistics: θ is a constant and not random, therefore it cannot be associated with a probability distribution, and so we cannot make probability statements about θ. How then do we proceed to make any inferences?

  • •

    The answer to this is to exploit the randomness in the data, X, as this is the only random variable in the problem. Before seeing the data, the estimator θ^MLE⁢(X) is a function of the random data, X. Therefore θ^MLE has a distribution and useful statistical properties, such as unbiasedness, standard errors and a sampling distribution.

Example: Drug Trial (continued)

In the case of our binomial example, we know from previously

E⁢[p^MLE] =p, Var⁢[p^MLE] =p^MLE⁢(1−p^MLE)n, n large⟹p^MLE ∼N⁢(p,Var⁢[p^MLE]).

Thus we can obtain, say, a 95% confidence interval for p as [0.46,0.91] — but what does this interval mean?

  • •

    But what is a 95% confidence interval for a parameter θ (such as p above)?

It cannot be the probability statement that θ lies in the interval with probability 0.95, as we know θ has no distribution.

  • •

    So what does the ‘95%’ figure correspond to?

  • •

    This leads to the second issue in this approach: as we cannot make direct inference about θ, we must exploit the randomness in X to make statements about θ^MLE, which by virtue of its relationship to θ can be interpreted as indirect inferences about θ itself.

  • •

    Thus, the frequentist interpretation of the ‘95%’ is associated with the sampling distribution of θ^MLE. So, if I were to repeat my experiment a large number of times, each time gathering a new data set and constructing a new confidence interval, then 95% of such intervals will trap the true value of θ within them.

  • •

    This is a consequence of interpreting probability as the long-run frequency of an event occurring in an infinite sequence of repeated experiments. From this basis, we develop methods and procedures that have long-run guarantees on their behaviour.

  • •

    The issue is, this indirect method of frequentist inference doesn’t actually say anything about whether the confidence interval you have actually constructed contains θ or not, and requires thinking about many other hypothetical data sets and confidence intervals other than the one in front of you. As these methods are typically based on large-sample results, we typically need big samples and small numbers of parameters for our results to be reliable.

  • •

    All of this raises the question of what the object of our analysis is. Conceptually, we’re doing this to use the data to learn about θ, but since only X is random, then this method can only tell us about θ^MLE⁢(X) and not θ.

The Bayesian approach to statistics

  • •

    The Bayesian approach to statistics is based on one key idea:

Fundamental Principle of Bayesian Statistics

Everything that is uncertain can be treated as random and be associated with its own probability distribution, provided we use a subjective interpretation of probability.

  • •

    Following this subjective approach55 5 Recall that the subjective interpretation of probability views probability as an individual’s quantification of their uncertainty of the event in question, thus representing some state of knowledge or belief., we can then treat the parameter θ as a random variable, with its uncertainty being described by a (subjective) pdf f⁢(θ).

  • •

    The likelihood of the data ℓ⁢(θ) can now can be fully viewed as the conditional probability distribution f⁢(x∣θ) of the data given the parameter.

Fundamental Procedure of Bayesian Statistics

The problem of “learning about θ from the data” then becomes trivial: use conditional probability with f⁢(θ) and f⁢(x∣θ) to find f⁢(θ∣x), which is the conditional pdf of the parameter θ given the data x. Thus we use the rules of probability (i.e. Bayes Theorem) to “learn” about our parameter from the data.

  • •

    The problems of being unable to make direct probability statements about θ in the standard Frequentist approach have now been resolved.

  • •

    We have a conditional probability distribution for θ informed by the data x, so we use this to answer all questions and make any inferential probability statements directly.

  • •

    Thus this approach allows us to directly ask the question we were trying to answer from the start:

What values of θ are most likely given the data under this model?

  • •

    To test any hypothesis, or make any statistical inference, all we need to do in the Bayesian approach is to write down all the relevant probabilities, and then condition them on any data (or other information) we have.

  • •

    In the Bayesian approach, large samples aren’t necessary for the methods to be valid and we don’t need to imagine many hypothetical replications of our experiments.

  • •

    However, in some cases with large amounts of data we will see that the results agree with standard Frequentist methods.

  • •

    While this may sound easy, it is not always straightforward to calculate the probability we need. The main criticism of the Bayesian approach is how we determine the values of all the component probability distributions in the calculation.

  • •

    In particular, the initial distribution for θ (known as the prior distribution) is a subjective choice, and it is one that is influential, often difficult, and sometimes controversial.

  • •

    Consequently, the Bayesian approach is criticised for the use of the “subjective” view of probability when science and mathematics should be an “objective” discipline66 6 However, every statistical model ever created in the history of the human race is still a subjective choice, and every assumption made in a standard statistical analysis was done so at the subjective choice of the analyst. So the pure objectivity of standard statistics could be debated (and has been extensively!).

  • •

    Finally, as the Bayesian approach introduces additional complexity by introducing a distribution for θ, its calculations are typically more complex and can often require extensive numerical computation.

  • •

    Some of the key differences between the standard and Bayesian views of statistics are summarised in Table 2. Some would say neither method is particularly ‘right’ or ‘wrong’, and which you use often depends on your goal and the nature of the problem.

  • •

    Given a large amount of good-quality data and a well-understood model then the Frequentist approach may be fine77 7 Some would argue that this is only because it approximates an underlying Bayesian approach, i.e. the one that is correct in terms of our scientific questions..

  • •

    If you have a small amount of data and a complex model with lots of unknown parameters, then a Bayesian approach will be a good idea.

  • •

    Regardless of the method you use or the interpretation you apply to a particular probability, the laws and theory of probability apply to both and do not change.

6.2 Revision: Conditional probability

  • •

    The key tenet of Bayesian inference is simply:

We use probability to describe all uncertainty.

Once we accept this, then the rest of how we proceed is fairly straightforward.

  • •

    If a parameter, θ, is unknown, that means we are uncertain about what its value is, and hence the right way to describe that uncertainty is through a probability distribution. Typically, the choice of that distribution is a subjective one.

  • •

    If the data, X, are unknown, then we express our uncertainty via a distribution parameterised by θ, giving us the likelihood for the data.

  • •

    If we want to use the data to ‘update’ or ‘learn about’ a parameter, then we use conditioning to find the conditional distribution of the parameter given the data, θ∣X.

  • •

    Thus, the basis of (almost) all Bayesian calculations is therefore the manipulation of conditional probabilities. We now review the key results and definitions of conditional probability for continuous random variables before we move on to the general statistical problem.

Information: Revision

Again, this section is mostly revision material. All of these results have been seen before in this course in the context of discrete random variables (Section 1.4.3), and in the Probability course in the context of continuous random variables.

  • •

    We will discuss the ideas of joint, marginal, and conditional probability densities, and then develop these ideas further to obtain continuous versions of the standard results (e.g. partition theorem, Bayes theorem) with which we are familiar in terms of discrete events.

  • •

    Let X and Y be two continuous random variables with joint pdf f⁢(x,y). Then the marginal pdf of Y is

    f⁢(y)=∫𝒳f⁢(x,y)⁢d⁢x. (96)

    and the conditional pdf of Y given X=x is

    f⁢(y∣x)=f⁢(y,x)f⁢(x). (97)

Definition: Multiplication rule

By re-arrangement of Equation (97), we can express the joint distribution of X and Y in terms of a conditional probability

f⁢(x,y)=f⁢(x∣y)⁢f⁢(y)=f⁢(y∣x)⁢f⁢(x)=f⁢(y,x). (98)

This is known as the multiplication rule.88 8 Note that the discrete version of this states P⁡[A,B]=P⁡[A∣B]⁢P⁡[B]=P⁡[B∣A]⁢P⁡[A]=P⁡[B,A],

This result generalises for multiple random variables X1, X2, …, Xn such that f⁢(x1,…,xn)>0, so we can write the joint probability as a running product of conditional probabilities:

f⁢(x1,…,xn)=f⁢(x1∣x2,…,xn)⁢f⁢(x2∣x3,…,xn)⁢…⁢f⁢(xn−1∣xn)⁢f⁢(xn), (99)

and a similar result holds for any permutation of the indices of xi.

  • •

    We can also condition the entirety of the multiplication rule on a further random variable Y to obtain the following supplementary result:

    f⁢(x1,…,xn∣y)=f⁢(x1∣x2,…,xn,y)⁢f⁢(x2∣x3,…,xn,y)⁢…⁢f⁢(xn∣y). (100)
  • •

    To obtain the continuous version of the partition theorem, we consider the joint distribution, f⁢(x,y), and the marginal distribution of Y, which is f⁢(y)=∫𝒳f⁢(x,y)⁢d⁢x. By substituting in the form of the joint distribution given by the multiplication rule (98), we obtain the desired result.

Definition: Partition theorem

By substituting the multiplication rule (98) into the marginal distribution (96), we can write the pdf of Y as:

f⁢(y)=∫𝒳f⁢(y∣x)⁢f⁢(x)⁢d⁢x, (101)

for a random variable X with f⁢(x)>0 and sample space 𝒳. This is the continuous version of the partition theorem99 9 Comparing to the discrete version of the partition theorem, P⁡[A]=∑bP⁡[A∣B=b]⁢P⁡[B=b], we note the correspondence between the two forms, though the summation has now been replaced by integration. as it is equivalent to treating the sample space of X as an (infinite) partition of the values of X

  • •

    Like the multiplication rule, the partition theorem can be conditioned on a further random variable, Z, giving the expression:

    f⁢(y∣z)=∫𝒳f⁢(y∣x,z)⁢f⁢(x∣z)⁢d⁢x (102)

    which is also given the name of summing over intermediate consequences, where x in this case are the intermediate consequences in question.

  • •

    We define X and Y as independent (X⟂⟂Y) if and only if f⁢(x,y)=f⁢(x)⁢f⁢(y). By expanding f⁢(x,y) via the multiplication rule we arrive at the equivalent definitions:

    f⁢(x)⁢f⁢(y) =f⁢(x,y)
    =f⁢(x∣y)⁢f⁢(y)
    ⟹f⁢(x) =f⁢(x∣y), (103)

    for f⁢(y)>0, and similarly for Y∣X.

  • •

    Recall that one interpretation of independence is that if X⟂⟂Y, then no matter what (or how much) I learn about Y, my pdf for (and hence my uncertainty about) X does not change. This is evident from Expression 103 above, since when we use conditioning to “learn about X from Y”, we construct f⁢(x∣y), however, under independence this is not affected by Y at all.

  • •

    A conditional version of independence can be defined by introducing an additional random variable.

Definition: Conditional independence

Suppose X, Y, and Z are random variables with f⁢(y,z)>0, then X and Y are conditionally independent given Z if and only if

f⁢(x,y∣z) =f⁢(x∣z)⁢f⁢(y∣z), f⁢(x∣y,z) =f⁢(x∣z), f⁢(y∣z,x) =f⁢(y∣z),

which is written X⟂⟂Y∣Z.

  • •

    The interpretation in this case is similar. Suppose that we have already observed the value of Z, then if X⟂⟂Y∣Z then no matter what additional information I gain about Y, my pdf for (and hence my uncertainty about) X does not change.

  • •

    The information in Z has told me all I need to know, and there is nothing that Y can tell me to cause me to change my probability distribution.

Definition: Bayes theorem for continuous random variables

Suppose X and Y are continuous random variables and f⁢(x)>0, then

f⁢(y∣x)=f⁢(x∣y)⁢f⁢(y)f⁢(x)=f⁢(x∣y)⁢f⁢(y)∫𝒴f⁢(x∣y)⁢f⁢(y)⁢d⁢y, (104)

where we have applied the partition theorem to the denominator to obtain the final equation1010 10 The comparison to the discrete form of Bayes theorem is obvious: P⁡[Y∣X]=P⁡[X∣Y]⁢P⁡[Y]P⁡[X].

  • •

    As with the other results, a conditional form of Bayes theorem can be obtained by conditioning everything on a third variable Z if f⁢(x∣z)>0:

    f⁢(y∣x,z)=f⁢(x∣y,z)⁢f⁢(y∣z)f⁢(x∣z).
  • •

    The essence of Bayes theorem is to invert the conditioning of probabilities,  i.e. to re-write f⁢(y∣x) in terms of f⁢(x∣y). Often, this is because the inverted form is a more natural variable to work with. For example, while P⁡[heart attack∣chest pain] may be difficult to determine, P⁡[chest pain∣heart attack] is easier.

6.3 Bayesian Statistics

  • •

    The Bayesian approach to statistics results from treating all unknown quantities as random variables and characterising their uncertainty via probability. Thus we can express a general Bayesian analysis in terms of the following stages:

Bayesian Stages

  1. 1.

    Prior: We have a collection of quantities, represented by θ, which could describe future data, X. θ may represent a parameter in a statistical model, index over many possible models, or a combination of both. We assign a prior distribution f⁢(θ) over the possible parameter values or models1111 11 When θ is discrete, we construct the prior distribution by directly assigning a probability to each possible discrete value of θ., which expresses our uncertainty about the value of the parameter or the appropriate statistical model, θ, before we see any data. This is often based on scientific insight, consideration of previous data/observations, and logic.

  2. 2.

    Data: We observe the data, X=x. Having observed x, we can now formulate the likelihood, f⁢(x∣θ), of seeing the data given the model or parameter value θ. This is the same as the standard likelihood ℓ⁢(θ), however, the meaning is quite different. In the Bayesian approach, θ is a random variable, so f⁢(x∣θ) is the conditional distribution of x given θ. In the frequentist approach, θ is not a random variable, so ℓ⁢(θ) is not treated as a density and is instead just a function returning the density of x for different parameter values.

  3. 3.

    Posterior: After seeing the data, we evaluate the likelihood of each parameter value or statistical model θ given the data x, and apply Bayes theorem to obtain posterior probabilities for each of the different parameter values or models. Thus we obtain the posterior distribution f⁢(θ∣x) of parameter (or model) θ. This expresses our uncertainty about the value of the parameter or choice of statistical model θ given the information we have learned after we have seen the data.

  4. 4.

    Inference: Using the posterior distribution, f⁢(θ∣x), the problem of inference becomes one of making statements about the posterior distributions, such as probability intervals, point estimates, or assessments of the probability of particular hypotheses.

  • •

    Clearly, the process of conditioning the parameter, θ, on the data, x, to “learn” from our observations is the key calculation in this approach to statistics. Since this requires reversing the conditioning in the likelihood to obtain the posterior, Bayes theorem is crucial, hence why this approach is known as Bayesian statistics.

Fundamental Equation of Bayesian Statistics: The Posterior

Any Bayesian statistical problem can be simply expressed as

f⁢(θ∣x) =f⁢(x∣θ)⁢f⁢(θ)f⁢(x), (105)
or in words, using the terminology above
Posterior =Likelihood×PriorData probability. (106)
  • •

    It is worth noting that no matter how large the data set or complex the model, all Bayesian approaches to statistical problems reduce to a calculation of this form.

  • •

    A simplification is possible by noting that once we are ready to calculate the posterior distribution, the data have been observed and we have learned that X takes the value x, a constant.1212 12 Before the data were seen they were random (or uncertain), but afterwards they are just the numbers we observed. Since x is just a constant for the posterior calculation, f⁢(x) must also be a constant, thus we can write:

Fundamental Equation of Bayesian Statistics: The Posterior (simplified)

f⁢(θ∣x) =f⁢(x∣θ)⁢f⁢(θ)f⁢(x)
=C×f⁢(x∣θ)⁢f⁢(θ)
⟹f⁢(θ∣x) ∝f⁢(x∣θ)⁢f⁢(θ)
or again in words
Posterior ∝Likelihood×Prior. (107)
  • •

    Often, we work with this simpler ‘proportional form’ of Bayes theorem, obtaining an unnormalised or improper posterior. As this relationship is only up to proportionality, the product on the right side of the expression does not integrate to 1, but to some C>0 instead.

  • •

    As a result, this proportional form is of no direct use if we wish to calculate probabilities – in this case, we must either use the full form of Bayes theorem to give a properly normalised density function, or subsequently renormalise the posterior.

  • •

    For simple problems, we can find f⁢(x) by applying the partition theorem to obtain:

    f⁢(x)=∫Θf⁢(x|θ)⁢f⁢(θ)⁢d⁢θ, (108)

    i.e. integrating (or summing) the posterior (107) over θ. Dividing (107) through by this value will yield a valid normalised posterior density again.

  • •

    In practice, however, doing the integral (108) for arbitrary priors and likelihoods is a very challenging numerical problem. The unnormalised posterior of (107) is then very useful in one of two ways:

    • –

      performing numerical methods to sample from f⁢(θ|x) despite f⁢(x) being intractable to express analytically (not covered in this course),

    • –

      to identify the functional form of the posterior distribution, and thereby spot if it corresponds to one of the standard distributions. In such cases, we can state f⁢(x) without the need for explicit integration at all (see Section 6.5).

Example: Drug Trial (continued)

Returning to the drug trial example, the number of patients whose condition improved while on the drug during the trial was described by X∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(16,p) – this is the likelihood for this problem with θ=p our parameter/quantity of interest. During the trial, we observed that x=11 patients improved – these are our data.

The probability parameter of the binomial distribution is not known, and so in the Bayesian approach we treat it as a random variable and must assign a prior pdf, f⁢(p). We know p represents a probability, so must be contained in the interval [0,1]. If we have no knowledge or information about possible values of p, it may be reasonable therefore to consider all possible values of p to be equally likely. Under this argument, we would use a prior of p∼U⁢[0,1], i.e. the uniform distribution.

Thus we have

Prior: f⁢(p) =1,p∈[0,1]
Likelihood: f⁢(x=11∣p) =(nx)⁢px⁢(1−p)n−x
=(1611)⁢p11⁢(1−p)5
Posterior: f⁢(p∣x) ∝1×(1611)⁢p11⁢(1−p)5
∝k⁢p11⁢(1−p)5,

for p∈[0,1], and we can find k by integrating and equating to 1 to get k=74256.

This illustrates the calculation of our posterior distribution for p given the data x=11. In fact, we will see later that this corresponds to a B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(12,6) distribution, so we can directly plot and compare our prior and posterior distribution for p and observe the effects of learning from the data. These plots are shown by the red curves in Figure 3.

It is clear that our initially vague prior for p has been transformed into something far more informative after updating by the data. The posterior distribution now has a clear mode (peak), located at p^=1116≈0.69 – same as the maximum likelihood estimate! Since the prior is completely flat the shape of the posterior is simply determined by the shape of the likelihood function, and so it is no surprise we obtain similar results. However, unlike the MLE, the posterior distribution is a distribution for p∣x and so we can ask the question: what is the probability that the drug has a generally positive effect? We could interpret this as asking what is P⁡[p>0.5], which we can find (by integration or using the statistics programming language   R  ) as 0.9283.

What if we thought p was more likely to take larger values rather than smaller,  i.e. our prior belief was that the drug was more likely to have a positive effect. We could express this by choosing a prior that was proportional to p. For example, an appropriate choice of density function could be f⁢(p)=2⁢p. We observe the same data and have the same likelihood, but the posterior for p∣x is now:

f⁢(p∣x) ∝2⁢p×(1611)⁢p11⁢(1−p)5
∝c⁢p12⁢(1−p)5,p∈[0,1]⁢and⁢c>0,

which, by a similar argument, we will later see corresponds to a B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(13,6) distribution. This prior and posterior are shown in Figure 3 by the blue curves. In this case, the posterior has a mode value of p~=1217≈0.71, which has shifted slightly upwards compared to the previous calculation - in fact, it is a compromise between the prior mode (1) and the likelihood mode (0.69).

6.4 The Prior Distribution

  • •

    The presence of the prior distribution in our calculations is one of the primary differences between the Bayesian and the likelihood approach to statistics, and as such it is often the most important issue for Bayesian methods 1313 13 And, for similar reasons, the main source of controversy surrounding adopting a Bayesian approach to statistics in general..

  • •

    Clearly we need a prior distribution for our parameters in order to apply the Bayesian methodology, and the results we obtain will be somewhat sensitive to that prior, so our choice of prior is important.

  • •

    In general, there are two types of priors:

    • –

      Informative priors – f⁢(θ) expresses specific knowledge or information about the behaviour of θ. In principle, we must (subjectively) choose or specify a distribution that represents our knowledge about θ, or else we must ‘elicit’ one from someone else. This is particularly difficult when θ is high-dimensional, or not well-understood.

    • –

      Non-informative priors (also known as diffuse, vague or objective priors) – f⁢(θ) is deliberately (and, in some sense, rigorously) vague about the behaviour of θ. The simplest such form is a uniform prior to express that all values of θ are equally likely. Typically, this leads to similar results to a frequentist likelihood-based analysis, as only the likelihood carries any information in the posterior. It is common to use uniform priors even if they don’t integrate to 1 (i.e. over all of ℝ) - such a prior is called improper. Use of improper priors can sometimes be acceptable as the posterior that results can turn out to be proper (though this opens another can of worms that we shall ignore).

  • •

    The distinction between, and use of, informative and non informative priors is another source of debate, though this time it is a debate between the Bayesians. In particular, critics would argue that incorporating subjective information into the problem is “not scientific”.

  • •

    Without getting into the fundamental philosophy behind all this, if we have prior information about the behaviour of θ then we should probably try to include that information into an informative prior. If we genuinely know nothing about θ, then a non-informative prior would be the appropriate choice.

  • •

    Another consideration relevant to our prior is convenience. Bayesian statistics for general problems with arbitrary priors and likelihoods requires explicit calculation of the conditional distribution, which will require substantial integration. With arbitrary distributions, these integrals are not guaranteed to be analytically tractable (i.e. there is no simple mathematical form for the posterior distribution). In such cases, the only approach is to perform some form of numerical integration which can be very computationally expensive.

  • •

    As a result, we may consider certain mathematical forms for the prior which, in combination with the likelihood, yields a mathematically convenient posterior.

6.5 Conjugacy

  • •

    For certain combinations of priors and likelihoods, the posterior we obtain is particularly mathematically convenient. Identifying and using such combinations can simplify the computation and analysis substantially.

Definition: Conjugacy

A conjugate prior distribution is one where the form of the posterior distribution is the same as the form of the prior distribution, that is, f⁢(θ) and f⁢(θ∣x) are pdfs belonging to the same family (e.g. they are both normal or they are both gamma). In which case we say

  • •

    f⁢(θ) is a conjugate prior for (or is conjugate with, or is closed under sampling from) the likelihood f⁢(x∣θ)

  • •

    the set of all such priors forms a conjugate family for (sampling from) the likelihood f⁢(x∣θ).

Comments:

  • •

    Conjugacy implies that the prior, f⁢(θ), and the posterior, f⁢(θ∣x), have the same functional form. For example, both could be Normal distributions. This relationship holds for all possible sample values and sample sizes. However, despite sharing a common type of distribution, the prior and posterior will differ in the parameter values of the common distribution.

  • •

    Clearly the form of the conjugate prior depends on the form of the likelihood. In other words, different data (or “sampling”) distributions have different conjugate prior distributions. In some cases there is no conjugate prior distribution.

  • •

    Conjugacy is a mathematical convenience which reduces the potentially difficult Bayesian update to a simple change in the parameters of the distribution from prior to posterior. We could use other priors, but obviously it makes the mathematics and the computation more complex. We should be mindful of the fact that we often choose conjugate priors to make the calculation simpler, not because it represents genuine prior information about the behaviour of θ.

Aside

A more formal definition of conjugacy goes as follows, though the above will suffice for our purposes.

Suppose that data x are to be observed with distribution f⁢(x∣θ). A family ℱ of prior distributions for θ is said to be conjugate (or closed under sampling) with f⁢(x∣θ) if for every prior distribution f⁢(θ)∈ℱ, the posterior distribution f⁢(θ∣x)∝f⁢(x∣θ)⁢f⁢(θ) is also in ℱ.

  • •

    To easily identify posterior distributions and to readily spot conjugacy, we introduce the following idea of the core of a distribution.

Definition: Core (or kernel) of a distribution

For a random variable X with pdf f⁢(x), if we can express its pdf f⁢(x) in the form

f⁢(x)=C⁢κ⁢(x),

where C>0 is a constant that does not depend on x, then we call κ⁢(x) the core (or kernel) of the density f⁢(x).

Lemma

Each core of a distribution, κ⁢(x), corresponds to a unique pdf, f⁢(x).

Proof

Following the definition above, let κ⁢(x) be such that f⁢(x)=C⁢κ⁢(x), where f⁢(x) is a valid pdf. For f⁢(x) to be valid, we must have that

∫−∞∞f⁢(x)⁢d⁢x=1⟹∫−∞∞κ⁢(x)⁢d⁢x=1C.

Now suppose there exists another valid pdf g⁢(x) which is also associated with κ⁢(x), so g⁢(x)∝κ⁢(x). If we write g⁢(x)=B⁢κ⁢(x), then

∫−∞∞g⁢(x)⁢d⁢x=B⁢∫−∞∞κ⁢(x)⁢d⁢x=BC.

For g⁢(x) to also be a valid pdf it must integrate to 1, which implies that we must have B=C. Therefore

g⁢(x)=C⁢κ⁢(x)=f⁢(x),

and so each κ⁢(x) is associated with a unique valid pdf f⁢(x).

6.6 Conjugate Bayesian analysis for binomial data

  • •

    To set up the general approach to Bayesian analysis of binomial data, we need to identify an appropriate prior for the probability parameter. The distribution we shall use is the Beta distribution, which is a very flexible distribution that is defined over [0,1], making it ideal for representing a probability.

  • •

    As we will see, the Beta distribution has a similar functional form as the binomial likelihood, so we will investigate it as an example of a conjugate prior.

Definition: Beta distribution

Let X∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a,b) for a,b>0 known. Then X has a Beta distribution with pdf

f⁢(x)=1B⁢(a,b)⁢xa−1⁢(1−x)b−1=Γ⁢(a+b)Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(b)⁢xa−1⁢(1−x)b−1,0≤x≤1

and 0 otherwise, where B⁢(a,b)=Γ⁢(a)⁢Γ⁢(b)Γ⁢(a+b) is the Beta function, and Γ⁢(a) is the Gamma function with Γ⁢(a)=(a−1)! for a∈N.

Properties:

  1. 1.

    The core of a B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a,b) pdf is

    κ⁢(x)=xa−1⁢(1−x)b−1
  2. 2.

    If X∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a,b), then

    E⁢[X] =aa+b, Var⁢[X]=a⁢b(a+b)2⁢(a+b+1).

    and

    M⁢o⁢d⁢e⁢(X)=a−1a+b−2⁢ for ⁢a,b>1
  3. 3.

    B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(1,1) is the same as U⁢[0,1],  i.e. f⁢(x)=1 for 0≤x≤1. Examples of the different shapes of the Beta density are shown by the coloured lines in Figure 4.

  4. 4.

    For a, b both large, then approximately X∼N⁢(E⁢[X],Var⁢[X]) (unless a≫b or b≪a).

  • •

    We have data X1, X2, …, Xn, where each Xi is 1 in the event of success with probability p, and 0 otherwise.

  • •

    Assuming the Xi are independent and p is constant, then our data are  i.i.d Bernoulli random variables with parameter p. If we only count the number of successes, X=∑iXi, then we have X∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(n,p).

  • •

    To find the posterior for p∣X, we need to combine the binomial likelihood with a prior for p. As the Beta distribution only has support over the interval [0,1], it is an ideal candidate for a prior for p.

Theorem: The Beta-binomial model

Suppose that we observe a random variable X=x where X∣p∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(n,p). If our prior distribution for p is such that p∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a,b), then the posterior distribution for p∣X is

p∣X∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a+x,b+n−x),

hence the Beta distribution is a conjugate prior for the Binomial parameter p.

Proof

We have a Beta prior and a Binomial likelihood, so assume we observe X=x successes. Then our posterior is:

f⁢(p∣x) ∝f⁢(x∣p)⁢f⁢(p)
=(nx)⁢px⁢(1−p)n−x×1B⁢(a,b)⁢pa−1⁢(1−p)b−1
∝pa+x−1⁢(1−p)b+n−x−1 (109)
∝pa~−1⁢(1−p)b~−1, (110)

where a~=a+x and b~=b+n−x.

So what distribution is this? From the properties of the Beta distribution given above, we recognise this as the core of a B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a~,b~)=B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a+x,b+n−x) distribution. Thus p∣x∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a+x,b+n−x) as required, and since the prior and posterior are both Beta distributions we conclude that the Beta distribution is indeed a conjugate prior for the Binomial parameter p. We can now write the posterior as:

f⁢(p∣x)=1B⁢(a+x,b+n−x)⁢pa+x−1⁢(1−p)b+n−x−1 (111)
  • •

    Note that now both the prior and the posterior are the same distribution, albeit with different values for their parameters.

  • •

    With a Beta prior and binomial sampling, the Bayesian update to p is simply: we add the number of observed successes, x, to parameter a, and the number of observed failures, n−x, to parameter b, and the corresponding Beta distribution is our posterior for p∣x. This is the convenience of conjugacy.

  • •

    Interpretation of hyperparameters: While we have identified a convenient functional form for our prior distribution, to specify a unique distribution for p we must choose values of a and b. There are various ways we could do this, however one approach is to notice where a and b appear in the posterior distribution (109). The parameter a is added to the number of observed successes x, and the parameter b is added to the number of observed failures n−x.

  • •

    We can therefore think of the prior distribution as representing an equivalent hypothetical prior sample of size (a+b) in which we have observed a successes. This allows us to attach a specific interpretation to the parameters a and b which can simplify the process of specifying a prior distribution.

  • •

    We also note that we can express the posterior expectation for p∣x as:

    E⁢[p∣x] =(a+x)(a+x)+(b+n−x)=aa+b+n+xa+b+n
    =aa+b⁢(a+ba+b+n)+xn⁢(na+b+n) (112)
    =E⁢[p]⁢λ+p^MLE⁢(1−λ), (113)

    where λ=(a+b)/(a+b+n).

  • •

    Our posterior expectation for p is therefore just a weighted average (i.e. a compromise, or convex combination) between our prior expectation, E⁢[p], and the maximum likelihood estimate, p^MLE. Thus we can think of the Bayesian posterior as being a compromise between the prior information and the information we gain from the data.

  • •

    Finally, we also note that, for n large, the value of λ in Expression (113) for E⁢[p∣x] is approximately 0, and so the prior mean has negligible impact on the value of the posterior mean. Thus, when n is large, the likelihood takes over the posterior and the prior has become irrelevant (since the likelihood conveys so much more information than the prior). As a result, for n very large, we get a similar value to that from conventional likelihood methods.

Example: Beta-Binomial Scenario for the Drug Trial

In the drug trial example, we considered two different priors f1⁢(p)=1 and f2⁢(p)=2⁢p. It is fairly straightforward to see that

f1⁢(p)=1 ≡B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(1,1)
and⁢f2⁢(p)=2⁢p ≡B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(2,1).

So our flat uniform prior for p is equivalent to observing one ‘prior success’ and one ‘prior failure’ to represent our lack of knowledge about p. Whereas f2⁢(p) placed more prior weight on larger values of p, and we see this is equivalent to 2 ‘prior successes’ and one ‘prior failure’.

Given we can express the priors as Beta distributions, it is then trivial to apply the Beta-binomial model, which gives the posteriors as

f1⁢(p∣x) =B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(12,6)
f2⁢(p∣x) =B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(13,6)

which are the same as we obtained before.

Comments:

  1. 1.

    a=b=1: this Beta prior corresponds to a uniform distribution for p. In other words, our prior beliefs are that all values of p are equally likely. Updating by the binomial likelihood arising from the observed 11 successes in a sample of 16 patients yields the posterior B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(12,6). This is illustrated in the left plot of Figure 5. The uniform prior (flat horizontal red line) carries no particular information on the value of p (it is seemingly non-informative, although there are subtleties here1414 14 The subtleties are that if we had worked with a different parameterisation e.g. θ2, and imposed a uniform distribution across θ2, we would have derived a different posterior. In other words, a uniform distribution is tied to the parameter we are using, so it is not truely “non-informative”.), so our posterior (higher-peaked green curve) just looks like a re-scaling of the likelihood (lower-peaked blue curve). In other words, with a non-informative prior the only information in the problem comes from the data.

  2. 2.

    a=5,b=0.5: this Beta prior corresponds to the belief that higher values of p are more likely than lower values, which is clear in the asymmetry of the red line (curving from bottom left to top right) in the right plot of Figure 5. In this case, although the likelihood (lower-peaked blue curve) is the same as before, the posterior (higher-peaked green curve) is no longer just a rescaling of the likelihood and instead is a compromise between prior and likelihood. The posterior is shifted slightly to the right and is more concentrated, placing more probability on larger values of p than for the previous case.

6.7 Bayesian inference

Critical Question: what is the point of all this?

So, we have seen the Bayesian approach in action, and how it delivers f⁢(θ|x), i.e. the posterior distribution for θ given the data x.

  • •

    Question: so what can we do with this? What does it give us?

  • •

    Answer: pretty much everything.

We can now answer any question about θ, and by extension about future measurements, probabilistically. This can then be used within Decision Theory (see the 3rd year course) to make optimal decisions under uncertainty. It is hard to overstate the importance of this capability.

  • •

    The posterior distribution summarises all of the information and uncertainty about our parameter, θ, given what we have learned from observing the data x.

  • •

    All of this information is encoded in f⁢(θ∣x). However, to make inference and answer questions we typically need to summarise this distribution (or its features) in a number of possible ways:

Information we can extract from the Bayesian Posterior f⁢(θ|x)

Simple summaries of f⁢(θ∣x)

– plots, location summaries (mean, median, mode), spread summaries (variance, quantiles), other characteristics (symmetry, number of peaks).

Probabilities

– use the distribution to directly calculate relevant probabilities, e.g. find P⁡[θ>a∣x], related to hypothesis tests.

Point estimates

– summarise the distribution in terms of a single “best” value of θ; often the same as the location summaries of the distribution.

Predictions

– use f⁢(θ∣x) to make predictions about some future data X∗ given θ and x.

Intervals and regions

– find intervals that capture a proportion of the possible values of θ, i.e. the interval [ℓ,u] where P⁡[ℓ<θ<u]=1−α.

6.7.1 Point estimates

  • •

    Point estimates are single values of θ that are, in some sense, a “best” value1515 15 (Non-examinable). Formally, to define a “best” value for θ we must have a particular mathematical criterion which this best value, θ^, optimises. Bayes point estimates define a loss function for any point estimate θ^, written L⁢(θ,θ^), which is small when θ^ is a “good” point estimate for θ. Different choices of functional forms of the loss function then lead to different values of the “best” point estimate θ^ when we optimise our expected loss. For example, the squared loss L⁢(θ,θ^)=k⁢(θ−θ^)2 leads to us using the posterior mean. obtained from f⁢(θ∣x). Thus the point estimate typically has some useful or meaningful properties associated with it. Two obvious choices are:

    1. 1.

      Posterior mode, or MAP estimate1616 16 MAP stands for “maximum a posteriori”, which is unnecessarily Latin., θ^MAP: this is the maximum of the posterior density, and is the obvious analogue to the usual maximum likelihood estimate (MLE), which maximises only the likelihood.

    2. 2.

      Posterior mean, E⁢[θ∣x]=∫θ⁢f⁢(θ∣x)⁢d⁢θ, is simply the posterior expectation with all of the usual properties and interpretations. This is the Bayesian analogue to what is called the least squares (LSQ) estimate.

Example: Drug-Inference continued

Let’s illustrate these different methods using the drug trial example from before. Recall that in a drug trial of 16 people, where each person had an unknown probability p of their condition improving while taking the drug. Thus we have a binomial likelihood X∼B⁢i⁢n⁢(16,p) and we observed that x=11 patients improved.

Using a flat uniform prior for p, p∼U⁢[0,1], we saw that our posterior for p∣x was B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(12,6). From the properties of the Beta distribution (recall that if Y∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a,b) then M⁢o⁢d⁢e⁢(Y)=(a−1)/(a+b−2) and E⁢[Y]=a/(a+b)), we can find the values of the possible point estimates to be as follows :

p^MAP =12−112+6−2=1116(=xn=p^MLE)
E⁢[p∣x] =1212+6=1218

Note here that when we use a flat uninformative prior distribution for p, our posterior distribution is just a re-scaled version of the likelihood and so the MAP estimate and the MLE estimate are necessarily the same.

However, if we consider the second prior for p, where f⁢(p)=2⁢p, then we found that p∣x was B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(13,6), and therefore that:

p^MAP =13−113+6−2=1217(≠p^MLE)
E⁢[p∣x] =1313+6=1319

where in this case we note that, because the prior places higher probability on larger values of p, our point estimates are, understandably, slightly larger than when the prior is flat.

6.7.2 Prediction (This section is Not Examinable: just for interest)

  • •

    Suppose that before we observed any data at all, we wanted to predict what the possible values of X could be. We would do this by finding the marginal distribution for X, which we also call the prior predictive distribution.

Definition: Prior predictive pdf

Before observing X, the prior predictive pdf for X is simply the marginal pdf of X, and can be expressed as

f⁢(x)=∫f⁢(x,θ)⁢d⁢θ=∫f⁢(x∣θ)⁢f⁢(θ)⁢d⁢θ,

where we have used the multiplication rule (98) in the last equality to introduce the product of the likelihood and prior.

  • •

    Now, suppose we have observed that X=x and we are interested in some future observation that we may have, X∗. Our prediction about the possible behaviour of X∗ given what we learned from the data is then captured by the distribution of X∗∣X=x.

  • •

    If X and X∗ represent observations of the same variable, we typically assume that they would have the same distribution expressed in terms of the same parameter, θ. This implies that X∗⟂⟂X∣θ, that is X∗ is independent of X given θ, since only θ informs us about the behaviour of X∗, and X is therefore only indirectly useful as we use it to learn about θ.

Definition: Posterior predictive pdf

The distribution of X∗∣X=x is expressed by f⁢(x∗∣x), and is known as the posterior predictive pdf, given by

f⁢(x∗∣x)=∫f⁢(x∗,θ∣x)⁢d⁢θ=∫f⁢(x∗∣θ,x)⁢f⁢(θ∣x)⁢d⁢θ,

When X∗⟂⟂X∣θ, we can simplify this as

f⁢(x∗∣x)=∫f⁢(x∗∣θ)⁢f⁢(θ∣x)⁢d⁢θ,

which is the integral of the product of the likelihood of x∗ and the posterior distribution for θ.

  • •

    What is happening here is that our predictive distribution for x∗∣x is effectively an average of all the possible distributions of x∗∣θ, with each one weighted by the posterior density of θ∣x. Thus the posterior predictive calculation accounts for all the possible uncertainty in θ, as well as accommodating what we have learned from observing x.

  • •

    Contrast this to the standard Frequentist approach to a prediction, which is to find a point estimate of the parameter (e.g. by maximum likelihood) to obtain a value θ^ and then to plug it into f⁢(x∗∣θ=θ^). Clearly, this approach ignores the entire range of possible values for θ∣x.

Example: Drug-Inference prediction

Question: Consider making a second drug trial of a further n=3 patients. Given the results of the first trial, what is the probability that the condition of all 3 patients improves when taking the drug?
Solution: Let X∗ be the number of patients in the new trial whose condition improves. The question is then asking for the posterior predictive probability P⁡[X∗=3∣X=11]. Applying the technique above, and using probability rather than density for the discrete random variables, we have

P⁡[X∗=3∣X=11] =∫01P⁡[x∗=3∣p]⁢f⁢(p∣X=11)⁢d⁢p
=∫01(33)⁢p3⁢(1−p)0×Γ⁢(18)Γ⁢(12)⁢Γ⁢(6)⁢p11⁢(1−p)5⁢d⁢p
=(33)⁢Γ⁢(18)Γ⁢(12)⁢Γ⁢(6)⁢∫01p14⁢(1−p)5⁢d⁢p
=(Γ⁢(18)Γ⁢(12)⁢Γ⁢(6))⁢(Γ⁢(15)⁢Γ⁢(6)Γ⁢(21))⁢∫01Γ⁢(21)Γ⁢(15)⁢Γ⁢(6)⁢p15−1⁢(1−p)6−1⁢d⁢p⏟=1
=Γ⁢(18)⁢Γ⁢(15)Γ⁢(12)⁢Γ⁢(21)=17!×14!20!×11!=14×13×1220×19×18
=0.319.

Alternatively, if we were to approach the problem in the standard statistical way, we would use the MLE from the first trial, p^MLE=1116 and plug that into the likelihood for X∗. So, what we would actually be calculating is

P⁡[X∗=3∣p=p^MLE]=(33)⁢p^MLE3⁢(1−p^MLE)0=0.325.

Clearly the two probabilities are different. Why? The standard MLE-based prediction can only consider one possibility for p, that is when p=p^MLE. However, the Bayesian predictive probability considers all possible values of p, as given by its posterior distribution, and averages over all those possibilities.

(End of non-examinable Section 6.7.2. All Material from here on is Examinable)

6.7.3 Credible intervals

  • •

    Credible intervals are the Bayesian analogue to confidence intervals, though their interpretation is more straightforward.

  • •

    Recall that a 100⁢(1−α)% confidence interval for a parameter θ is interpreted as meaning that with a large number of repeated samples, 100⁢(1−α)% of the corresponding confidence intervals calculated from those samples would contain the true value of θ.

  • •

    In other words, the confidence interval itself is a realisation of a pair of random variables (L⁢(X),U⁢(X)) where

    P⁡[L⁢(X)<θ<U⁢(X)]=1−α,

    where we emphasise that here θ is the fixed but unknown variable (in the Frequentist sense) and (L⁢(X),U⁢(X)) are random variables.

  • •

    Thus we see that for some fixed unknown θ, the endpoints of the interval are random variables as they are functions of the random unknown data X. Thus the confidence interval is derived from the distribution of X1717 17 Not θ, as it is a constant which cannot have a distribution in this standard Frequentist approach to statistics., and so is constructed using the likelihood function f⁢(x∣θ).

  • •

    Conversely, a 100⁢(1−α)% credible interval is an actual interval derived from the distribution of θ such that it contains the parameter θ with probability 1−α. This is arguably a much clearer and much more useful interval object.

Definition: Credible interval

A 100⁢(1−α)% credible interval [ℓ,u] for a random variable θ∈ℝ satisfies:

P⁡[ℓ≤θ≤u]=P⁡[θ∈[ℓ,u]]=1−α.

Similarly, a 100⁢(1−α)% credible interval for θ given the data X=x satisfies:

P⁡[ℓ≤θ≤u∣X=x]=P⁡[θ∈[ℓ,u]∣X=x]=1−α.

This is often referred to as a 100⁢(1−α)% posterior credible interval.

  • •

    Note that the endpoints of the interval (ℓ and u) are now the constants, and it is θ which is now random.

  • •

    If θ is a vector of parameters, then we can define this more generally as a credible region, which is a set C such that P⁡[θ∈C]=1−α.

Types of credible intervals

  • •

    Our definition of a credible interval doesn’t identify a unique interval for θ. There are many (possibly infinitely many) ways of positioning the credible interval [ℓ,u] such that P⁡[ℓ≤θ≤u]=1−α (unless α=0). We consider two standard ways to define a credible interval consistently:

Definition: Equal-tailed and Highest (posterior) density Credible Intervals

  1. 1.

    Equal-tailed (EQT) intervals — this interval is constructed such that P⁡[θ<ℓ]=P⁡[θ>u]=α/2, so there is an equal probability of falling in the lower tail of the distribution as there is in the upper tail. If θ has a standard distribution, we can use its cumulative distribution function (cdf) Fθ and its inverse to find these values, as Fθ⁢(ℓ)=α/2 and Fθ⁢(u)=1−α/2.

  2. 2.

    Highest (posterior) density (HPD) intervals — this interval (or region) is the narrowest possible interval (i.e. |u−ℓ| is smallest) that we could construct which has P⁡[ℓ≤θ≤u]=1−α. Such an interval contains the regions of highest density.

  • •

    The difference between equal-tailed and highest posterior density intervals is illustrated in Figure 6. These two definitions give the same interval if the pdf is symmetric and has one peak (unimodal). See also Figure 7 for a direct comparison, showing how different the EQT and HPD intervals are for a non-symmetric but uni-modal Gamma distribution.

Example: Drug-Inference, Credible Intervals.

To find equal-tailed credible intervals exactly, we need to find the inverse cdf for θ∣X. We can find this analytically for simple pdfs by integrating and re-arranging, or we can use the (free) statistical software environment   R  and its functions for standard distributions. For the drug trial example, our posterior distribution is a Beta and so we can use the  qbeta  function to find ℓ and u.

Suppose we wish to find the 95% posterior credible interval for the drug trial example when our prior was f⁢(θ)=1. We said previously that this posterior distribution was θ∣x∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(12,6). Thus a 95% posterior equal-tailed credible interval is constructed by finding the 0.025 and 0.975 quantiles of this distribution. Using   R  , we find that

> qbeta(0.025,12,6)
[1] 0.4404173
> qbeta(0.975,12,6)
[1] 0.8579025

and so our 95% EQT CrI is [0.440,0.858]. Note that if this distribution was one for which we had standard tables, we could use those instead of   R  to find the interval endpoints.

We summarise the results of the calculations for 95% prior and posterior credible intervals for θ in the table below.

f⁢(θ) 95% EQT CrI f⁢(θ∣x) 95% EQT CrI 95% Approx Normal CrI

width=0.95 width=0.417 width=0.424

6.7.4 Normal approximation to Credible Intervals

  • •

    Obviously, if we know the distribution of θ, and can find its cumulative distribution function easily (by integration, tables, or   R  ) then we can calculate the credible interval [ℓ,u] exactly.

  • •

    However, often - just as in frequentist confidence intervals - we can adopt a normal approximation to compute the credible interval.

Definition: Approximate Normal credible intervals

Given a random variable θ, an approximate 100⁢(1−α)% credible interval for θ is given by

E⁢[θ]±zα/2∗⁢Var⁢[θ]

Often, this calculation will be done using the posterior distribution of θ∣X, and so would use the expectation and variance under that posterior distribution instead:

E⁢[θ∣x]±zα/2∗⁢Var⁢[θ∣x]
  • •

    Using such a normal approximation is justified in the case where the distribution for θ is unimodal, symmetric and ‘well-peaked’, or when a Normal approximation is valid given the nature and parameters of the distribution of θ (e.g. if θ is B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(a,b) with a,b large).

  • •

    Note that this is still just an approximation to the interval made for convenience; using the exact distribution will always yield more precise results.

  • •

    Note that this interval may look just like a frequentist confidence interval, but because it is computed from the mean and variance of the Bayesian distribution for θ, rather than the sampling distribution of the statistic, it can be quite different from the corresponding confidence interval.

Example: Drug-Inference Normal Approximation for Credible Intervals

Lets illustrate the Normal approximate CrI for the posterior distribution θ∣x∼B⁢e⁢t⁢a⁢(12,6) in the drug trial example.

To find the approximating Normal distribution, we require the mean and variance of the posterior distribution. These are

E⁢[θ∣x] =1212+6=0.6666667, Var⁢[θ∣x] =12×6(12+6)2⁢(12+6+1)=0.01169591.

So, our approximating Normal distribution is N⁢(0.6666667,0.01169591). The approximate 95% Normal credible interval is then simply

E⁢[θ∣x]±zα/2∗⁢Var⁢[θ∣x] =0.6666667±1.96×0.01169591
=[0.4547012,0.8786321].

The other 95% approximate Normal credible intervals for θ are summarised in the final column of the table in the Example above.

6.8 Conjugate analysis for Normal data

  • •

    Our final example of a conjugate family is for the case when the data are Normally distributed.

  • •

    The conjugate prior family of distributions for the mean, μ, is itself Normal.

  • •

    As with standard frequentist methods, how we deal with the problem depends on whether we treat the variance σ2 as known or unknown.

  • •

    We will look at the case where σ2 is assumed known.

  • •

    Now, before we begin, we highlight that the following calculations become rather messy if we try to work with the Normal distribution expressed in terms of the population variance, σ2, in the usual way. To make life easier, we consider instead the precision, which is the reciprocal of the variance.

Definition: Precision

The precision, τ, of a random variable X is defined as the reciprocal of its variance

τ=1Var⁢[X]=1σ2.

So, if X has high precision then it has a low variance, and vice versa.

  • •

    So, let X∼N⁢(μ,σ2) and define the precision as τ=1σ2, then we can write X∼N⁢(μ,1τ) and its pdf as

    f⁢(x∣μ,τ)=τ2⁢π⁢e−τ2⁢(x−μ)2.

Theorem: The Normal-Normal model, with known variance

Let X1,…,Xn be  i.i.d N⁢(μ,σ2=1τ) with precision τ>0 known. Suppose our prior pdf for μ is N⁢(m,v2=1t) with t>0, then our posterior pdf for μ∣x1,…,xn is also normal such that

μ∣x1,…,xn∼N⁢(m1,v12=1t1),

where

t1 =t+n⁢τ, andm1 =t⁢m+n⁢τ⁢x¯t+n⁢τ=t⁢m+n⁢τ⁢x¯t1.
  • •

    Note that we can re-write the posterior mean as

    m1=E⁢[μ∣x1,…,xn]=tt1⁢m+n⁢τt1⁢x¯=k⁢m+(1−k)⁢x¯,

    where k=t/(t+n⁢τ). Thus again the posterior mean is a weighted average of the prior mean, m, and the sample mean, x¯, and weights proportional to the respective precisions.

  • •

    The data precision is n⁢τ, which if we reintroduce σ2 is just nσ2=1σ2/n – i.e. the precision of the sample mean x¯. Note that each additional data point we observe increases our data precision by τ.

  • •

    The posterior precision is then just the simple addition of the prior precision, t, to the data precision n⁢τ. Since these precisions combine additively for normal samples, we obtain simpler expressions for precision than we would obtain for variance.

  • •

    We find the posterior variance, v12, of μ by taking the reciprocal of the precision t1:

    v12=1t1=1t+n⁢τ=11v2+nσ2=(v⁢σ)2n⁢v2+σ2=v2⁢(σ2n⁢v2+σ2),

    which is clearly more ugly than the expression for the precision.

  • •

    Before we prove the conjugacy theorem above, we need to find the core for a Normal density, X∼N⁢(μ,σ2=1τ). As the random variable is X here, we only care about the terms in x and so we find the following:

    f⁢(x∣μ,σ2) ∝exp⁡{−12⁢σ2⁢(x−μ)2}=exp⁡{−τ2⁢(x−μ)2} (114)
    Additionally, we can multiply out the quadratic inside the exponential to get
    f⁢(x∣μ,σ2) ∝exp⁡{−12⁢σ2⁢(x2+μ2−2⁢x⁢μ)}
    ∝exp⁡{−12⁢σ2⁢(x2−2⁢x⁢μ)}=exp⁡{−τ2⁢(x2−2⁢x⁢μ)}. (115)

Proof: The Normal-Normal model, with known variance

First, note that the normalising constant of a Normal distribution, 1/2⁢π⁢σ2, does not depend on the mean μ, so we can just absorb it into the proportionality constant immediately. Thus our likelihood takes the form

f⁢(x1,…,xn∣μ,τ) =∏i=1nf⁢(xi∣μ,τ)
∝∏i=1nexp⁡{−τ2⁢(xi−μ)2}
=exp⁡{−τ2⁢∑i(xi−μ)2}.

We can rewrite ∑i(xi−μ)2 as (the full calculation is left as an exercise for the reader):

∑i(xi−μ)2=∑i(xi−x¯+x¯−μ)2=⋯=∑i(xi−x¯)2+n⁢(x¯−μ)2,

where the first term is constant for a given sample as it is purely a function of the data. So, our likelihood in terms of μ is given by:

f⁢(x1,…,xn∣μ,τ)∝exp⁡{−n⁢τ2⁢(x¯−μ)2}.

Our prior pdf for μ is also Normal, giving

f⁢(μ∣m,t)∝exp⁡{−t2⁢(μ−m)2}.

Thus our posterior pdf for μ∣x1,…,xn is proportional to the product of the likelihood and prior:

f⁢(μ∣x1,…,xn) ∝f⁢(x1,…,xn∣μ)⁢f⁢(μ)
∝exp⁡{−n⁢τ2⁢(x¯−μ)2}⁢exp⁡{−t2⁢(μ−m)2}
∝exp⁡{−n⁢τ2⁢(x¯−μ)2−t2⁢(μ−m)2}
∝exp⁡{−12⁢[n⁢τ⁢(μ2−2⁢μ⁢x¯+x¯2)+t⁢(μ2−2⁢μ⁢m+m2)]}
∝exp⁡{−12⁢[(n⁢τ+t)⁢μ2−2⁢(n⁢τ⁢x¯+t⁢m)⁢μ+(n⁢τ⁢x¯2+t⁢m2)]}
∝exp⁡{−n⁢τ+t2⁢[μ2−2⁢μ⁢(n⁢τ⁢x¯+t⁢mn⁢τ+t)]}
∝exp⁡{−t12⁢(μ2−2⁢μ⁢m1)}.

From (115), this is the core of the Normal density N⁢(m1,1t1) as required.

Example: Water Contamination

A process for testing water contamination by a particular agent produces samples that are normally distributed, with mean μ and standard deviation σ=135 (so precision is τ=1/1352). Prior beliefs about μ are normal with mean m=750 and a 95% probability that 250<μ<1250.

  • •

    The probability statement above is equivalent to saying that for a prior standard deviation of v, then 1.96⁢v=500, thus v≈250 and our prior precision is thus t=1/2502.

  • •

    To estimate μ, we take n=18 independent samples, giving values with mean x¯=603.22.

  • •

    By the above theorem for conjugate normal priors to a normal likelihood, we have that μ∣x1,…,xn is N⁢(m1,v12=1t1) where

    t1 =t+n⁢τ=12502+181352=1.004×10−3
    so⁢v1 =1t1=31.56
    and⁢m1 =n⁢τt1⁢x¯+tt1⁢m=605.53.
  • •

    A posterior 95% credible interval is therefore:

    m1±1.96⁢v1 =605.53±1.96×31.56
    =[543.67,667.38].
  • •

    How big a sample n do we need so that the width of the posterior 95% credible interval for μ∣x1,…,xn is ±20?

  • •

    We want 1.96⁢v1=20, so v1≈10. Therefore

    t1=1100=t+n⁢τ=12502+n1352,

    so we need n≥181.96.

  • •

    Suppose that to satisfy health standards we require the contamination to be below a value of 600. What is P⁡[μ⁢<600∣⁢x1,…,xn]?

    P⁡[μ⁢<600∣⁢x1,…,xn] = P⁡[μ−m1v1⁢<600−m1v1∣⁢x1,…,xn]
    = P⁡[Z<−0.1752]=0.4305.
  • •

    This shows that we can now apply Bayesian methods to the case of normal data, provided we are happy to specify a normal prior.

  • •

    This Normal-Normal framework is pretty flexible and hence has been widely employed across a large range of subjects.

  • •

    This concludes the Bayesian section and indeed the whole course: I hope you have enjoyed it!
